en: *Fanggui*, Scroll Three, Part Two, concluded by the Śramaṇa Zhiyan of Zhixiang Monastery on Mount Zhongnan.
Within the Fifth Stage (*pañcamī bhūmi*), the six sections are the same as before. First, regarding the explanation of the name: one attains the supramundane.
Because one possesses wisdom and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and is thus able to cross over what is difficult to cross, it is called the "Difficult to Conquer" (*Sudurjaya*) stage.

Regarding that which is abandoned: according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is the obstacle of pride regarding the purity of the body; according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it is the parinirvāṇa of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
Ignorance (avidyā) further possesses two obstructions:

first, the contemplation that takes birth-and-death and nirvana as being mutually exclusive; second, the failure to cultivate the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas) subsumed under skillful means.
Furthermore, it counteracts the two types of karmic obstructions and the single causal condition for retribution, which is birth-and-death.
That which is manifested by the three vidyās is the meaning of the continuity being non-different.
That which is accomplished by the four vidyās is the perfection of dhyāna and the training in the Four Noble Truths.

That which is attained through the five vidyās is the merit of the continuity being non-different, characterized by the thorough penetration of the dharmadhātu; it is the attainment of the fruit of the dharmakāya, which is indistinguishable from that of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, and the accomplishment of the five stages (bhūmis).
The *nairmāṇika-phala* (fruition of emanation) is the same as before.
Regarding the sixfold explanation of the text, there is a general classification into three parts:
first, the verse praising its arising; second, the explanation of the essence of the stages (*bhūmi*); and third, the verse concluding the preceding section.
The first fifteen verses are as follows:

first, two verses on the Bodhisattva’s joyful cultivation of the three types of worship; next, two verses by the Heavenly Kings praising the Buddha and Bodhisattvas for their untainted merits; next, ten verses by the celestial maidens praising the perfection of both causes and fruits—the application of great compassion; and finally, one verse of liberation requesting the manifestation of entry into subsequent realization.
Regarding the text on the Goddess, the first seven verses praise the cause; the next two verses extol the fruit; and the subsequent one reveals that practice as the means of realizing the cause.

There are three aspects to the essence of the stages (*bhūmi*): first, the antidote to superior pride; second, the excellence of the practice of the non-abiding path; and third, the excellence of its fruit.
The preceding text has two parts concerning the two types of pride (*māna*): first, pride regarding one’s own stage (*svabhūmi-māna*), and second, pride regarding other stages (*parabhūmi-māna*).
Regarding "other stages," this refers to attaining supramundane knowledge within the first four stages and taking up their superior characteristics, which is termed pride.
The ten kinds of pure mind are employed as the remedy for two types of pride within one's own stage:
first, the pride that seeks superior characteristics among these ten; second, the pride that takes this seeking itself as a basis for further conceit.
As the remedy for these, one practices in accordance with the path of suchness.
In these two passages, they are both collectively termed "superior pride" (*adhimāna*), as their function in counteracting pride is identical.
The first passage has three parts:
first, it reiterates the preceding section to introduce the subsequent one, and exhorts the practitioner to cultivate entry into it.
Second, the exposition of the ten minds;
third, the conclusion regarding the accomplishment of benefits from the passage beginning with "The bodhisattva, by means of this...

Furthermore, those who share the same mind of non-retrogression are identical in that their expediently purified mind and their mind of realized non-retrogression both take the correct principle as their object without distinction.

Furthermore, regarding the "seven purities" mentioned in the text: first, purity of precepts; second, purity of concentration; third, purity of view; fourth, purity by overcoming doubt; fifth, purity of the path and non-path.
These five are designated by the same names in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions.
The latter two are distinct from the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

Regarding the latter two: the first is called "purity through practice" (*caryā-viśuddhi*) and the second is called "cessation through practice" (*caryā-prahāṇa*), because in that [Lesser Vehicle] school, the ultimate goal is cessation.

As for the names in the Mahāyāna: the first is called "cessation through practice," and the second is called "the progressive purity of the factors conducive to enlightenment through reflection" (*bodhipakṣya-dharma-cintā-uttarottara-viśuddhi*), because this school relies upon the cessation through practice to give rise to the supreme aspiration.
Although there are seven practices, the text contains six phrases.
Within the third phrase, there are two kinds of purity: namely, purity of vision and practice (*dṛṣṭi-carita-viśuddhi*), and purity by crossing over doubt (*tīrṇa-kāṅkṣā-viśuddhi*).
The remaining characteristics can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the stages (*bhūmi*): according to the Hīnayāna, these consist of the stage of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) prior to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*); followed by the three [moments] of the path of vision; followed by one [moment] of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); and finally, one [moment] of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).

Regarding the *Treatise on the Three Stages of the Mahāyāna*, the "Cultivation of Severance" (*xingduan*) and the "Cultivation of Abiding" (*xingzai*) are contained within the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); all other aspects are identical to those previously mentioned, as explained in the *Great Commentary* (*Dashi*).
Second, following the practice in accordance with Suchness (*tathatā*) has three parts:

first, a general manifestation of the practice in accordance with Suchness by raising the preceding [topic] and initiating the subsequent; second, a specific clarification of the characteristics of the practice in accordance with the path of Suchness, beginning from "attaining the great vow" (*mahāpraṇidhāna*); and third, a general conclusion, beginning from "giving rise to certainty and non-retrogression."
Regarding the first general section, there are three aspects of the essence of the Dharma and four distinct categories of phrases.

As for the three aspects of the essence of the Dharma: first, the factors of the path cultivated in the four stages; second, the ten kinds of pure minds prior to this stage; and third, the practice in accordance with the Way toward Suchness within this stage.
The four sections of the text may be understood accordingly.
Regarding the section on "not abiding in the path," the sutra text contains two parts:
first, the enumeration and analysis of the real dharmas of the Four Noble Truths, which constitutes the practice for one's own benefit that guards against afflictions.
The second is the differentiation of transforming sentient beings; this is the protection of the altruistic practice of the Hīnayāna.
The preceding sūtra has two parts:
first, the differentiation of the real dharmas of the Four Noble Truths; [second, the differentiation of the stages of practice].
Following this, based on these four clarifications, the ten gates of contemplation (*daśa-vipaśyanā-mukha*) are explained through the method of analytical exposition (*vibhāga*).
This text consists of two parts:
first, the listing of the ten names; second, the sequential explanation of the text.
Within the gateway of the Four Noble Truths, the meaning encompasses the entire Dharma-realm; therein, the Bodhisattva exhaustively illuminates everything without omission.

Although the divergent theories following various wisdoms are so vast and distinct as to be difficult to fathom, for now, we shall briefly establish ten gateways based on the perfection of a single numerical category.

However, these ten gates are known by the Bodhisattva himself; because the characteristics of such self-knowledge are difficult to clarify, they are manifested through the medium of emanation to reveal their distinction. This is merely using emanation to manifest self-knowledge, so that it may be subsumed under the name "purity of wisdom regarding all knowable phenomena."
Regarding "opening and closing": these ten gates are, in total, only one, differentiated through the transformation of sentient beings.
If categorized according to the capacity of those to be transformed, they are divided into two:
the first nine transform those of small capacity, and the last one transforms those of great capacity.
The manifestations that arise according to the needs of transformation are divided into three categories:

the first five transformations cause sentient beings to develop understanding; the next four transformations cause them to initiate practice; and the final transformation causes them to enter realization.
According to the differences among persons, [the teaching] is divided into seven:

first, converting those whose faculties are not yet mature; second, converting those whose faculties are already mature; third, converting those who harbor doubts regarding the profound Dharma; fourth, converting those who have erroneous understandings of the Dharma; fifth, converting those who have strayed from right mindfulness; sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth, converting those with right view; and tenth, converting those of the Mahāyāna who are capable of being transformed.
According to the differences in the dharmas, these are divided into ten; if analyzed extensively, their specific enumerations are immeasurable.
Regarding the distinction between the general and the particular in relation to the actual dharmas: each of these ten gates applies universally to each of the four preceding truths.
First, regarding the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one universally contemplates the distinct characteristics of the four truths.
Regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one universally contemplates that the essential nature of the four truths is empty and quiescent.
As for the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-satya*), one universally contemplates that the four truths are neither existent nor non-existent.
Regarding the distinction between them: the former involves a general observation that the four truths differ in their respective existence or non-existence.

The latter, which speaks of the establishment of the truths, involves a general observation of the characteristics and phenomena of the four truths as they are integrated through dependent origination.
Regarding the "truth of phenomena" (*vastu-satya*), it refers to the general delusion regarding the four truths that results in the occurrence of suffering and other such states.
Regarding the "truth of arising" (*utpāda-satya*), it refers to the general delusion regarding the four truths that gives rise to the accumulation [of karma] (*samudaya*).
"Exhausting non-arising" means universally understanding the Four Noble Truths and attaining the realization of cessation (*nirodha*).
"Entering the Path" means universally understanding the Four Noble Truths and achieving the Path (*mārga*).

Regarding the Bodhisattva-Tathāgata stage as the perfected truth: it thoroughly penetrates the four truths and the true nature of dependent origination—the pure realm—and constitutes the cause and fruit of the Mahāyāna path.

Furthermore, regarding these truths: the first four truths directly clarify that the essence and nature of the Dharma-realm are nothing other than the four truths; the subsequent four truths concerning phenomena and so forth indicate those things that are not the four truths; the intermediate five truths represent the sequence of skillful means for cultivating the characteristics of understanding and contemplation; and the final single truth clarifies the perfect, all-pervading self-substance of the Dharma-realm—the wondrous path of complete cause and unobstructed virtue fully endowed.

When distinguishing the characteristics of the dharmas according to the conditions of the teachings: first, the Four Noble Truths directly clarify the essence of the dharmas; next, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) clarify their characteristics; next, the truth of characteristics clarifies the characteristic of the single true truth; and finally, the truth of differentiation clarifies the phenomena of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Regarding the establishment of the truths: it clarifies that because ordinary beings are deluded and inverted, they take this very nature of the dharma-realm to be afflictions; thus, the three realms flourish and blaze forth in the world, and a multitude of characteristics accumulate and arise.
Next, the four truths of phenomena are explained to clarify the skillful means of correct cultivation as an antidote.

However, these are not merely the four truths; rather, they are the skillful means of correct cultivation for Bodhisattvas. Because these dharmas are universal and not restricted, even those of the Two Vehicles can cultivate progress within them, and even the wholesome karma of humans and devas operates within this practice.

Now, because this bodhisattva has perfected the path of skillful means for correct cultivation as an antidote, he is able to manifest the unobstructed path whose essence is perfectly complete and coextensive with the dharma-realm; thus, it is intended to clarify the sequential entry into the Tathāgata’s wisdom and truth within the stages of a bodhisattva.
This contemplation follows the meaning of the treatise.

Regarding the statement that "the wisdom of resolute belief and understanding (*adhimukti-jñāna*) is not known by the wisdom of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*)," this explains the preceding passage on the Tathāgata’s truths; it means they are known through causal wisdom, not through the resultant wisdom of exhaustion.
Furthermore, it may be said that the *āgama* of words and letters is known through faith and wisdom, rather than being known by the inexhaustible wisdom of the ineffable meaning.
This text merely distinguishes them in terms of understanding.
Regarding the further refinement of the text within the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottaraparivarta*), this is a simplification based on practice.

The commentary explains that "wisdom like a mirror-image" refers to the accomplishment of tasks through meditative concentration prior to the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) of the Three Vehicles; it is like a reflection in a mirror, wherein the accomplishment of tasks is sovereign.

Its stage is not fixed; it may be seen as the four wholesome minds such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, or the four concentrations such as "Light" (*āloka-labdha*) and so forth, or the forty minds prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), or the ten practices (*caryā*) and ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), or even from the time of mundane cultivated wisdom (*laukika-bhāvanā-prajñā*) until the attainment of concentration—these are its stages.
The second [section], "Protecting the Lesser Vehicle through Diligent Expedient Means," is divided into two parts:

first, observing that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are false, deceptive, and delusive, thereby giving rise to thoughts of compassion and loving-kindness for sentient beings; second, from the passage "Having attained such wisdom" onwards, the specific elucidation of compassion and loving-kindness.
This passage has two parts:
first, it clarifies the vow to transform others; second, from the phrase "contemplating all conditioned phenomena as they truly are" onwards, it clarifies the mind that transforms others.
This [second] part also has two sections:
First comes compassion (*karuṇā*), and subsequently, from the passage "In this way, suffering and affliction, etc.," the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is explained.
The text on compassion has two parts:
first, the preparatory means for generating compassion; second, from "Knowing sentient beings," the actual elucidation of the contemplation of compassion.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, observing suffering as it truly is to know the essential nature of suffering; second, from the passage "Furthermore, he thinks... onwards, observing profound and heavy suffering.
This section reveals faults through the perspective of sentient beings, clarifying their pitiable state.
Within the section on profound and heavy suffering, the text contains two parts:

first, observing sentient beings who undergo suffering with strange persistence, yet do not know to feel weary of it or seek liberation; second, from the phrase "because of ignorance and delusion" onwards, clarifying the reasons why sentient beings are so strangely persistent.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, an explanation of profound suffering; second, from the passage "In this way, birth and death... onwards, an explanation of its heavy suffering.
In the commentary on the text concerning loving-kindness (*maitrī*), there is a general division into two parts:

The first is to cultivate wholesome dharmas for the sake of sentient beings; the second, from "contemplating in this way" onwards, is to generate vows for their benefit according to what they have cultivated.
The initial section has two parts:
the first concerns the beginningless evil thoughts toward sentient beings; here, the third, fifth, and sixth phrases of the sutra text are missing.
Second, "I alone shall gather the wholesome dharmas";
second, among the vows for the benefit of others, the first is general and the latter nine are specific.
Although the textual sequence here is not strictly chronological, there is no loss of meaning if one interprets the text according to its logical order.
The commentary on the section concerning the fruits is broadly divided into four parts:

first, the excellence of encompassing merit; second, the excellence of spiritual cultivation; third, the excellence of teaching and transforming sentient beings; and fourth, the excellence of giving rise to wisdom that accords with the world.

The first two are one's own practice; they are the fruit of the purity of the knowledge of what is to be known at the highest level. Regarding the inclusion of merits, these are accomplished through one's own nature (*svabhāva*), while those of superior progress are accomplished through the excellence of cultivation.

The latter two concern benefiting others; these are the fruits of the diligent skillful means for benefiting sentient beings mentioned previously: the practice of transforming others through those who excel at transformation, and the wisdom of transforming others through those who accord with worldly knowledge.
The remainder of the text may be understood.

Within the fourth section on "knowledge that accords with the world," there are two parts: first, a general explanation of its intent; second, a detailed explanation of the wisdom of transformation beginning from the phrase "knowing all that exists in the world.
Within this detailed explanation, there are ten points:

1. Knowledge of writing and so forth; 2. Knowledge of the nature of stones and so forth; 3. Methods for treating illnesses; 4. Composing treatises and so forth; 5. [Knowledge of] the sun, moon, and so forth; 6. Observing the precepts and so forth; 7. Matters that do not cause harm to living beings; 8. Matters that bring peace and happiness to living beings; 9. Emerging out of compassion; 10. Gradually causing them to believe and enter the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma.
In the third [section] of the Sūtra, two phrases are missing; in the fourth meaning, not a single phrase is present; the remaining text is as in the Śāstra.
Furthermore, the Śāstra is difficult to understand regarding the shifting manifestations of auspiciousness and misfortune, entry and so forth, according to the times.
The characteristic of the body being pervasive is the mark of the certainty of retribution.

There are eight marks of transformation according to time: first, the sun; second, the moon; third, the stars; fourth, the planets; fifth, the clouds; sixth, the smoke; seventh, the mist; eighth, the dust.
The moon is the second;

the stars are the third—by "stars" is meant the five planets: Jupiter in the east, Venus in the south, Mercury in the west, Saturn in the north, and Mars in the center; these constitute the five planets.

As for the "four lodges," they refer to the twenty-eight lunar mansions (nakṣatras), such as Aśvinī, Bharanī, and so forth; because the five planets dwell within them, they are called "lodges" (siddha).
Earthquakes are five;
dreams are six;
perceptions are seven.
Auspicious and inauspicious phenomena constitute eight categories; the "fox-cry" and other such omens are all subsumed under these auspicious and inauspicious classifications.
Furthermore, the "seven luminaries" refer to the sun, the moon, and the five planets.
"Entering" means following in accordance.
The karma of the eight phases of the past life follows in accordance with the fruit signified by the eight phases of the future life.
Furthermore, the various marks throughout the entire body are the signs of the fruits of love and non-love resulting from fixed retribution.

Furthermore, regarding the five practices in relation to the five defilements: the precepts remedy the violation of precepts; the four dhyānas remedy sensual desire; the supernormal powers remedy false refuge; the four immeasurables remedy the deluded practice of killing living beings and performing sacrifices to seek merit; and the four formless absorptions remedy the deluded cultivation of liberation and the heterodox practices of external paths.
Regarding the section on the fruits of this stage, the three fruits are the same as those previously mentioned.
The "portion on flexibility" (*mṛdu-bhāga*) consists of four parts:

first, the characteristics of flexibility; second, the purity of the wisdom of the teaching, beginning with the passage "Furthermore, like the sun and moon"; third, the specific practices of the stage; and fourth, the concluding summary of these characteristics.
The sūtra omits the third phrase.
The initial passage explains the principle; next follows the analogy; finally comes the application.

First, it clarifies that seeing the Buddha serves as the condition for initiating practice; next, it shows the ability to refine practice; and finally, it shows the purity resulting from such refinement.

Within the practice of refinement (*pariśodhana*), first comes making offerings, next the cultivation of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), and finally the reception of the practice of the Dharma (*dharmacaryā*).
The sutras are often insufficient [in their detail].

Furthermore, within the fourth and fifth stages (*bhūmi*), the fruit of renunciation (*pravrajyā*) is contained within "gentleness" (*saṃvṛtatva*). Why is this? Because from the fourth stage onward, one attains supramundane, untainted practice (*anāsrava-caryā*), and thus the meaning of renunciation becomes manifest.
The remaining meanings should be understood as they appear in the treatise.
Regarding the three sets of verses, the first explains the intended meaning;
the second clarifies the phrasing of the stanzas, which consists of thirty-nine [verses]:

The first eleven verses praise the excellence of pride; next, thirteen verses praise the excellence of the non-abiding path; next, seven verses praise the non-abiding fruit; next, seven verses praise the three topics beginning with pliancy; and finally, one verse concludes them.
Regarding the section on "Surpassing Pride within the Path": the first two verses concern equanimity, while the subsequent nine verses concern practicing in accordance with the path.

Regarding the section on "Not Abiding within the Path": the first four verses concern the purity of wisdom, while the subsequent nine verses concern the textual account of diligent skillful means for benefiting sentient beings.
Within the sixth stage, there are six sections as before.

First, regarding the explanation of the name: because the great wisdom of the practice of *prajñāpāramitā* manifests with uninterrupted presence, it is called the "Manifestation Stage" (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).

Regarding the second, that which is abandoned: according to the *Dichilun* (Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya), it refers to the subtle habitual tendencies of afflictions; if following the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha), it refers to the ignorance of subtle marks and activities. This text places this [abandonment] in the seventh stage.
Furthermore, there are two obstacles:
first, the realization that all phenomena arise and continue in succession, which is delusion regarding the conventional;
second, the frequent arising of conceptualizations of marks, which is delusion regarding the ultimate.
Furthermore, it treats two types of karmic obstructions and one type of birth-and-death caused by retributive conditions;
third, it elucidates the meaning of being neither defiled nor pure;
fourth, it distinguishes what is accomplished, namely the perfection of prajñā and the realization and attainment of dependent origination.

Regarding the five fruits obtained: they consist of the merit of penetrating the suchness (*tathatā*) of the twelvefold dependent origination as being neither defiled nor pure; obtaining the purity of the continuum; and being able to purify the defiled turbidity of the fruits of all sentient beings, as well as the six stages (*bhūmi*).
The fruit of penetration is the same as previously described.

Regarding the sixfold explanation of the text, there are three parts: first, the verses praising the arising; second, the exposition of the essence of the ground (*bhūmi*); and third, the verses concluding the preceding section. The first part consists of eighteen verses:

the first two verses consist of the Bodhisattvas’ praise; the next two consist of the threefold offering of the devas; the next two consist of the praise of the meaning of the ground by the celestial kings and their retinues; the next eleven consist of the goddesses’ praise of the essence of the ground and its various specific practices; and the final one consists of the request for liberation to enter the subsequent realization.
The section on the women is divided into three parts:
first, one verse on making offerings of music; second, nine verses praising the virtues of the fruit and the cause; and third, one verse on silently gazing at the Buddha.
Within the first nine verses, the initial four praise the fruit, while the subsequent five praise the cause.
There are three parts to the text:
first, the practice of great compassion; second, the practice of the six perfections; and third, the conclusion establishing its virtuous function.
Within the section on the essence of the stages (*bhūmi*), there are three major divisions:
First, the antidote to the pride of superiority; second, the excellence of the practice of non-abiding on the path; third, the excellence of its fruit.
The first section has three parts:
first, citing what precedes to introduce what follows, and exhorting one to enter into practice.
Second, the analysis of characteristics;
third, the conclusion on the accomplishment of practice.
Regarding the first, clarifying the antidote to superior pride, it explains the ten dharmas of equality, which have two intended meanings:
First, the sphere of understanding; second, the sphere of practice.

Regarding the "sphere of understanding," these ten gates constitute the dharmas that serve as the standard; from the section on "Non-abiding in the Path" onwards, it clarifies the skillful means of the contemplative gates that constitute the basis for practice.

Regarding the "objects of speech and action," these refer to the ten equalities, which constitute the initial stage of contemplative understanding (*guan-jie*). The section beginning with "not abiding in the Path" clarifies the characteristics of perfected contemplation.
Furthermore, it is also appropriate to separately determine the textual divisions according to the *Śāstra*.
Regarding the ten kinds of equality, there are two ways of explaining their characteristics:
first, one general [equality], followed by nine specific ones.
Within these nine, there are three [categories]:

The first seven [verses] use non-existence to refute existence; the next one uses existence to refute non-existence; and the next one refutes both existence and non-existence simultaneously. The first section has three parts:

the first is the gate of liberation of emptiness, which is the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-vipaśyanā*); the next five are the gate of liberation of signlessness, which is the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda-vipaśyanā*); and the final one is the gate of liberation of wishlessness, which is the contemplation of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva-vipaśyanā*).
Regarding the sequence of practice: this refers to the external completion of practice through understanding.
A doubt arises:
"If all phenomena are non-existent, how can they endure for a long time and remain definitively established?"
To answer this doubt, the sutra states: "Because they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
To say they lack intrinsic nature means they have no real nature.
Furthermore, it asks: "If all phenomena do not exist, how is it that they are perceived as truly existing?"
To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra states: "All phenomena are signless and equal.
Furthermore, a doubt arises:

"If phenomena are signless, why is it that in some places phenomena arise and in others they perish? Why does the grasping mind follow what it perceives rather than acting according to its own will? How can they be signless?"
To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra states: "All dharmas are equal in their non-arising.
From here on, it concerns the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*); because it is not like the absence of marks (*animitta*) and so forth, it differs from what preceded.
Regarding the term "non-arising": all phenomena arise from thought and possess no independent existence; how, then, can they be said to exist?
As the treatise states, this is because thoughts arise in a continuous succession.
Furthermore, it is said:
"If a phenomenon arises from mindfulness, then its causes and conditions are not singular.

I do not perceive any such conditions as mindfulness and the like; I perceive only the established phenomena that have been produced. Since I do not perceive mindfulness and the others, they must be non-existent; yet the phenomena produced by them should be said to exist."
To refute this doubt, the Sūtra states: "Because there is no production.
As for the statement that there is no production: since phenomena arise from others, you do not perceive them as being produced from conditions.
Since you have already conceded that phenomena arise from others, yet you do not perceive this characteristic, you should know that what you perceive is precisely that [arising from others].
You claim that you do not apprehend a real object, but rather that it is produced by false perception; therefore, the treatise says: "Non-arising is equal."
These two are delusions regarding the Truth of Suffering.
Furthermore, it is said:
"If all phenomena arise from another and lack the nature of arising from themselves, I admit that they do not exist."
Since the causes capable of bringing about [a result] have already established the other, this potent capacity should be said to exist.
To answer this doubt, the Sūtra says: "Because all things are detached, all dharmas are equal."
This relies on the eighth phrase of the Sūtra.

Regarding the term "detachment" (*viveka*): it refers merely to the fact that the objects grasped by conceptual attachment are deemed real; yet when one examines what is seen by those [grasping], there is nothing from which they arise:
first, because they do not exist prior [to perception]; second, because they lack any real principle.
How is this known?

If something arises from conditions, it is merely apparent and not real; therefore, we know that what is perceived is but a mark (nimitta) and lacks intrinsic existence. Thus, the treatise says: "Because it is a defiled mark."
"This is precisely the conceptualization of the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya).
Question:
"If it is the Truth of Origination, it is then subsumed within the aggregate of consciousness (citta-skandha)."
If cognition already exists within the object, how should it be gathered? Answer:
When one discusses the nature of the grasper, it should be understood as appearing in accordance with its conditions.

The functioning of afflictions and karma is reckoned to exist within objects; yet those objects are themselves non-existent. Since their meaning ultimately reduces to the grasping of signs, this is called "origination" (*samudaya*).
Furthermore, it is said: "Regarding the causal conditions of all phenomena, if one investigates their beginning and end, neither can be grasped."
Investigating this meaning, the defiled dharmas depend upon reality; they arise from delusion regarding the truth, and thus may be said to be non-existent.
The two truths—the conventional and the ultimate—which constitute the truth of cessation that is the object of such delusion, ought to exist in accordance with principle.
Answer: You claim that the ultimate and the conventional accord with principle and are therefore real;
this argument is not correct.
The cessation and the path, as well as the ultimate and the conventional, are the domain of the sublime conduct and correct wisdom; why then do you say that "suchness" is real?
To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra says: "It is primordially pure and equal."
If one asserts that these are real, then a defiled mind arises; thus, it cannot be said that they are originally pure. Therefore, the treatise states, "Because of the characteristic of purity.
This refers to delusion regarding the two truths of cessation and the path.
Furthermore, it is said:
If phenomena were not as they appear—that is, if they did not exist as real entities—then worldly discourse would not arise.
Since we currently observe that names are diverse and different, this serves as proof that the referents of those names are not non-existent.
Answer: As for the statement that the names grasped by conceptual attachment are not one, this refers to worldly designations (*prajñapti*), which did not previously exist as real entities.
How is this known?

We merely observe that in the world there are cases where the meaning is obtained but the name is not, and cases where the name is obtained but the meaning is not; thus we know that names do not invariably follow from meanings.
Your claim that meanings truly give rise to names and so forth is mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and is not ultimately real.
To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra states: "Because there is no conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Names do not exist substantially; they arise dependent upon meanings.
Meanings do not manifest of themselves; they are revealed by relying upon names.
This verifies that these are the causes and conditions of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Furthermore, when observing the cause that is the meaning, one does not see the effect that is the name;
and when observing the effect that is the name, one does not see the cause that is the meaning.
This semblance of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is likewise non-existent; therefore, the treatise states, "because it is a characteristic of discrimination (*vikalpa*).
The reason for speaking only of discrimination is to reveal that its very characteristic is empty.
This refers to the names of the four truths, which were already explained above in the context of the contemplation of non-arising.
Furthermore, it says:
"I have known that characteristics are non-existent and have realized that arising is not real; thus it is verified that one can proceed with certainty toward reality as it is."

Answer: If you claim that your own view is false and non-existent, while another view—free from conceptual thought—is something to be grasped, this is still merely discrimination. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Because there is neither grasping nor abandoning."
Regarding "no grasping or abandoning": this was originally based on emotional conceptualization; these perceived objects of grasping are all unreal.

Now, returning to the view that being free from thought is the goal, this too is identical to the previous delusion; thus the Treatise says, "because of the characteristics of emerging and submerging."
The reason why only "appearing and disappearing" is mentioned is that appearing and disappearing are themselves emptiness.
Thus far, the non-existent has been used to dispel the existent.
Furthermore, it says:

I subsequently examined the arising of these signs and found them to be non-existent; furthermore, I realized that apart from conceptual thought, they do not exist. One should know that phenomena such as defilement and purity, or the ultimate and the conventional, have no intrinsic substance and are not objects toward which one can proceed.
Answer: Your view that defilement and purity are not subject to progression and therefore constitute non-existent dharmas is incorrect.
To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra says: "Like illusions, dreams, and so forth."
If phenomena were entirely non-existent, why would there be places where one dreams and places where one does not?
By examining this, one knows that all phenomena are not definitively non-existent; therefore, the treatise says: "I do not have the characteristic of existence."
The reason for refuting the self by stating not merely that "there is no self" is that this serves to distance one from the self while avoiding abiding in a state of non-self.
Since things are produced through conditions like illusions, this differs from the aforementioned views; it is precisely by means of existence that non-existence is refuted.
It further states:
"The reason why the eight types of views were previously raised was that they did not exhaust the principle, as they used non-existence to refute existence.
Furthermore, the one view that subsequently arose also did not exhaust the principle, as it used existence to refute non-existence."
I now maintain that my body cannot be characterized as exclusively existent or nonexistent; rather, it fully possesses both meanings, which accords with reason.
Response:
As is seen externally, this does not transcend the realm of sensory perception.
How is this known?
It is because the objects as they appear are such that "non-existence" is not distinct from "existence," and "existence" is not distinct from "non-existence.
According to their underlying principle, non-existence is itself existence, and existence and non-existence are one.
To dispel this doubt, the Sūtra states: "Existence and non-existence are non-dual.
To say they are non-dual means that phenomena do not abide of themselves, but arise in dependence upon conditions.
Furthermore, because it is not a condition (*pratyaya*), it constitutes the dharma of fruition.
Upon examining all dharmas, they do not transcend the categories of self and other; since neither self nor other abides, emptiness is established through the very facts of existence.
If one perceives them as having existence or non-existence, this arises from not transcending the two limits of self and other; thus the treatise says: "Because of formation and destruction."
The reason why only formation and disintegration are mentioned is that formation and disintegration are themselves emptiness; therefore, one does not seek them separately.
One should know that this is the dharma of non-duality and equality: it is not by eliminating existence and non-existence that non-duality is spoken of; this is precisely suchness.
This verifies that what are called "existence" and "non-existence" are termed conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Nor is a separate dharma established within the two dharmas of existence and non-existence to constitute "non-duality. One does not grasp them together as identical; for in the law of dependent origination, existence and non-existence share the same essence and neither possesses intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Because one speaks of that non-existent dharma as being existent, existence is itself non-existence;
conversely, because one speaks of that existent dharma as being non-existent, non-existence is itself not non-existence.
Because existence is not separate from non-existence, there is no external duality of "existence" and "non-existence";
because non-existence is not separate from existence, there is no external duality of "non-existence" and "existence. Therefore, it is said that existence and non-existence are non-dual.

Furthermore, it is taught that the dharmas of existence and non-existence are non-dual; yet, even this non-duality has no self-nature that can be grasped. This refutes the dualistic clinging to both existence and non-existence.
Regarding the third section, the concluding text, there are two points to be known; their meaning and characteristics are as explained in the treatise itself.

The preceding section clarifies the phenomena that serve as the object of training by means of the twelve bases (*āyatana*); the following section distinguishes the meditative gateways upon which one relies by means of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Question:
Since the preceding section clarifies phenomena solely in terms of the twelve bases, why do the various meditative gateways in the following section focus exclusively on dependent origination?
Answer: The categories of "comprehending phenomena" (*dharmasaṃgraha*) are broad in scope; therefore, they encompass both the environment and its inhabitants by means of the twelve bases (*āyatana*).

Now, however, we are dealing with the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanāmukha*), where external objects are subsumed under the internal; thus, it is restricted to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
This passage consists of two parts:
first, the elucidation of non-abiding with reference to the initial dwelling, which establishes the general thesis;
second, from the words "He forms this thought" onwards, the opening of the gates of contemplation based on that actual dwelling, which constitutes the specific explanation.
Because the preceding stages are inferior, it is only while dwelling in the middle stages that one is called "non-abiding";
because this stage is superior, one is called "non-abiding" even while first dwelling in the stage.
The first section has two parts:
1. "Contemplating the characteristics of phenomena" (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and so forth recapitulates what preceded and introduces what follows.

Regarding the phrase "characteristics of phenomena," it recapitulates the ten equalities of phenomena mentioned in the preceding text; by following this recapitulation, one enters the sixth stage. This is based on the *Śāstra*, and the *Sūtra* may be inferred accordingly. 2.
From "Furthermore, by means of superior great compassion" onwards, the non-abiding is explicitly revealed.
Within this, the first six lines below provide an analysis:
first, explaining the name. Because it follows the preceding contemplations, this is called "furthermore" (*punar*).

Regarding "Great Compassion as the Foremost": it refers to the mind that keeps sentient beings in mind; to extract them from suffering is "compassion" (*karuṇā*), and when compassion increases, it is termed "great" (*mahā-*) [compassion].

Regarding the increase of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*): when the mind seeks pity, it is termed "increased" (*adhimātra*). Furthermore, because one seeks the supreme fruit (*adhiphala*), it is called "supreme. Because one seeks the Buddha-wisdom in order to benefit sentient beings, it is named "great compassion."

Regarding "fulfillment" (*paripūri*): it means being free from the conditioned mind and, out of weariness with the conditioned, investigating dependent origination; to investigate it until its ultimate limit is called fulfillment.
This is where the Sūtras and Śāstras differ in their presentation.
According to the treatise, there are four propositions:
namely, the single phrase "arising and ceasing" of the fourth [proposition] constitutes the mode of activity based on the preceding three gates.
According to the sutra text, the third [proposition] is precisely "arising and ceasing," whereby arising and ceasing itself serves as the fulfillment of the contemplation.
Based on two locations in the sūtras and śāstras, there are two interpretations of the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*):

First, according to the śāstra, it is held that both the sentient beings and the causal conditions for bodhi are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Since one now knows this through wisdom, it is called "contemplating arising and ceasing.

Second, according to the sūtra, the dharma of causal conditions arises in forward order and ceases in reverse order; since its primary purpose is to save sentient beings, it is called "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*).
Furthermore, if one relies on the sūtras, it can also be understood that four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) may be established.

Second, to clarify the meaning of the sequence of the three minds: having mounted upon the preceding contemplation of emptiness, one then reflects that sentient beings are entangled in delusion; therefore, compassion arises first.
Because of this compassionate reflection, one seeks the wisdom of the Buddha with the desire to benefit others; thus, the second [mind] arises.
The Buddha’s wisdom is necessarily accomplished through the departure from faults; therefore, the third [wisdom] arises.
These three are distinguished according to self-benefit and benefit for others: the first is for the benefit of others, while the latter two are for self-benefit.

The four [applications of mindfulness] protect against afflictions and protect against minor discrimination; the first two protect against minor [discrimination], while the last one protects against afflictions.
Regarding cause and effect, the first and last encompass the cause, while the second seeks the fruit.
Sixth, non-abiding in conceptualization: the first [of the two] benefits others by not abiding in nirvana;
the latter two benefit oneself by not abiding in the world.

Second, regarding the correct abidings, there is a separate analysis of the contemplative gates (*vipaśyanā-mukha*): the first provides a general overview of the contemplative gates according to the sūtras and śāstras, while the second explains their meaning.

The first section has three parts: first, a topical analysis according to the *sūtra*; second, a topical analysis according to the *śāstra*; third, a comparative analysis of the text by correlating the *sūtra* and the *śāstra*.
Within the topical analysis according to the *sūtra*, there are two sections: first, a detailed explanation of the ten contemplations; second, a summary conclusion thereof.
What are these ten contemplations?

1. The sequential order of the causal factors (*nidāna*); 2. From "The three realms are false" onwards, clarifying that they are subsumed within the one mind; 3. From "Ignorance has two kinds" onwards, clarifying the assistance and completion through one's own karma; 4. From "Ignorance causes formations (*saṃskāra*) not to cease" onwards, [clarifying] their inseparability; 5. From "Ignorance, craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*)" onwards, clarifying the activity of the three paths; 6. From "Ignorance and formations belong to the past" onwards, clarifying the contemplation of the prior and subsequent limits; 7. From "From ignorance and formations up to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*)" onwards, clarifying the accumulation of the three types of suffering; 8. From "With ignorance as a causal condition, formations arise" onwards, distinguishing the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of causes and conditions; 9. From "The causal condition of ignorance is the bondage of birth" onwards, distinguishing the bondage of the arising and ceasing of causes and conditions; 10. From "The causal condition of ignorance is the conformity to existence (*bhava*)" onwards, this is the contemplation of the exhaustion of non-existence through conformity.
Within each of these, there are both forward and reverse contemplations, which constitute two [aspects].
Such is the text of the Sūtra.
Second, the topical analysis according to the Śāstra.
Within these ten stages of contemplation, the treatise analyzes them through three gates:

first, contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination from the perspective of a mind that feels weary of and seeks to transcend conditioned existence; this corresponds to the previously explained "Gate of Arising and Ceasing" in its full completion.

Second, regarding the section "Deeply contemplating sentient beings and observing the twelve links of dependent origination within the mind," it is explained as the contemplation that accords with compassion (*karuṇā-anuloma-bhāvanā*).
As for the term "accordance" (*anuloma*), this refers to giving rise to compassion in accordance with dependent origination; thus, the aforementioned compassion serves as the primary basis.

Third is the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination with the mind seeking Buddhahood; in the treatise, this is termed the "contemplation of the differentiation of all-aspect wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā-vibhāga-bhāvanā*), which is precisely the aforementioned contemplation predominant in compassion.
Question:

Previously, in the section on the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), compassion was explained first, followed by the superior [virtues], and finally the fulfillment of compassion was revealed. Why is it that here, the fulfillment is explained first, followed by compassion, and finally the superior [virtues]?
In the previous section on the stages of generating the mind within the first abiding (*prathamavihāra*), compassion was presented first and its fulfillment discussed later;
however, here, in accordance with the sequence of actual practice (*pratipatti*), compassion’s fulfillment is presented first, followed by the discussion of its intensification (*adhipati*).
What is the meaning of this?

In the preceding first stage (*ādikarmika-bhūmi*), one contemplates the emptiness and quiescence of phenomena through the ten superior dharmas; because one then reflects that sentient beings are entangled by falsely perceived conditioned phenomena, compassion arises first.
Since compassion seeks to uproot suffering, one must attain the Buddha-wisdom; thus, the superior resolve (*adhyāśaya*) arises next.
The Buddha necessarily achieves realization by departing from existence; therefore, the contemplations on the fulfillment of arising and ceasing are elucidated.
Now, within the actual practice, one begins by departing from faults, first cultivating weariness toward conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*);
because one has personally departed from faults, one then reflects that sentient beings remain therein without emerging, and subsequently distinguishes the stages of compliance.
The first two encompass the causes; logically, they must come first.
The knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the practice for seeking the fruit; logically, it must come last.
Within these three gates, there are ten types of contemplation on the collection of causes and conditions (*hetupratyayasamudaya*) each, totaling thirty.
Within each gate there are both regressive and progressive sequences, thus forming sixty.

The preceding analysis has clarified these sixty instances solely based on the stages of abiding; when contrasted with the subsequent stage of fruition, there are one hundred and eighty gates of causal-condition contemplation.

We know this to be so by examining the divisions of the text and analyzing the collection of conditions through the three gates of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), for each of these gates subsumes different elements.
As the Sūtra says: "By relying on the liberation of emptiness, one attains the ten samādhis of emptiness; the same applies to the signless (*animitta*) and the wishless (*apraṇihita*)."
Based on these three kinds of emptiness, there are three meanings.
If one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination through the samādhi of emptiness, then all twelve links are empty. How is this known?

The Master has already discussed distinguishing the signless as being aligned with the samādhi of emptiness: if one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination through the gate of the signless, the twelve links appear as illusory;
if one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination through the gate of wishlessness, the arising of conditions is seen as real.

The treatise further states that the gate of signless contemplation (*animitta-vipaśyanā*) corresponds to the nature of reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); because reality is free from signs, it is thus assigned to it.

Signless contemplation is paired with non-arising (*anutpāda*), as the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is non-arising and there is nothing therein to be sought after; therefore, it is used for this correspondence.
These causal conditions and the dharma-gates of similarity and difference may be understood by reflecting upon them according to the ten emptinesses and three samādhis explained below.
Regarding the third point, the demarcation between the treatise and the sūtra text, there is yet another specific meaning.

Based on the ten sections of the preceding sūtra text, one immediately forms the contemplations on the causes and conditions of wearying detachment from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and so forth; therefore, according to the ten sections of the preceding and following sūtra texts, there are one hundred and eighty gates.
He asked again:
"If, according to the sūtras and śāstras, there are no sixty gateways of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-lakṣaṇa*), how can one hundred and eighty gateways be established?
He replied:

Since the Sūtra initially opens with three gates of contemplation, the Master of the Treatise (Śāstrakāra) subsequently maintains that the original Sūtra consists of twenty sections, while further distinguishing other categories such as the three gates, four gates, and nine gates.

Having previously opened the gates of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) to verify the essence of contemplation within the subsequent sutras, one knows that there are certainly sixty gates.

Now, correlating the treatise with the sutra, the ten gates are subsumed into three sections; the intent is to cultivate weary detachment from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) through a single contemplation, the details of which will be further analyzed below.

However, regarding the way this treatise subsumes the divisions of the sutra: within the contemplation of revulsion toward the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it subsumes the ten contemplative gates found within that sutra. These are taken as the first gate among the thirty, which is designated as one and called the "Characteristics of the Accomplished Answer" (*siddhānta-lakṣaṇa*).
Next, there is a half-gate which is again taken as one and called the "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha*).
Finally, the remaining eight gates and a half are combined into one and called the "Distinctions of Conventional Truth" (*saṃvṛti-viśeṣa*).
Within the second great compassion, the contemplation of conformity, ten items are subsumed into four:
the first section constitutes one, called "contemplating the ignorance and perversion of sentient beings";
the next one constitutes another, called "seeking liberation elsewhere."
The next three are combined into one, termed "seeking liberation through heterodox paths";
the final four are combined into one, termed "seeking a distinct liberation.
Within the analytical contemplation of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), these ten are subsumed into nine:
First, one and a half sections are taught as a single unit, named the Contemplation of Defilement and Purity;
next, one section and a half are again treated as a single unit, named the Contemplation of the Basis of Defilement;
following that, there are five sections, each treated separately as a single unit.
Next, two gates are combined into one, named the "Contemplation of Beginninglessness";
next, one remains as one, named the "Contemplation of Diversity. Together with the preceding ones, there are nine.
Within these three gates, the sequence of the text may vary; they shall be explained individually later.

Second, regarding the explanation of the meaning: according to the root text of the Great Sūtra, the dependent origination of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is manifold; now, by means of essential gateways, it is briefly subsumed into two categories:
first, distinguishing dependent origination with respect to the defiled dharmas of ordinary beings; second, clarifying dependent origination with respect to the pure portion of bodhi.
Regarding the classification according to the gates of purity, they are summarized into four types:

first, innate existence; second, that which is produced through cultivation based on innate existence; third, that which is produced through cultivation alone; and fourth, that which is innate based on what was produced through cultivation.

Regarding the term "originally existent": the fundamental reality of dependent origination is essentially free from conceptualization; the *dharmadhātu* is manifest and remains unmoving throughout the three periods of time. Thus, the *Xingqi pin* (Chapter on the Arising of Nature) states: "Within the minds of sentient beings there are scrolls of scripture as numerous as motes of dust, and there is the great tree of Bodhi, which all the sages together testify to."
Human perception differs between the past and the present, yet the tree itself does not distinguish between them; thus, we know it has existed from the beginning.
Furthermore, this text on dependent origination shows that the twelve links of dependent origination are themselves the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the statement that cultivation arises from what is originally present: although all pure dharmas have no distinct nature from the beginning, they now arise as new virtues through various conditions. Since these conditions are themselves produced by delusive phenomena, true wisdom must instead accord with the essential body of Samantabhadra.

Fundamentally there is no discrimination; the wisdom cultivated is likewise without discrimination. Therefore, this wisdom accords with principle and does not follow various conditions. Thus one knows that what is produced through cultivation arises from what is originally possessed, emerging as being of the same nature. Hence, the "Chapter on Nature" states: "It is called the bodhicitta because it is the arising of the nature."

Question: Since "cultivation arising from the fundamental" (benyou xiusheng) is something newly initiated, its meaning is not that of something old; why, then, do you say it proceeds from its "fundamental nature" (benxing)? Answer:
This chapter explains the meaning of "newly arising" as referring to that which is produced through cultivation; because it is closely related to its original nature, it arises from that nature.

Just as today's grain is not distinct from the grain at the beginning of the eon, it accords with its original nature and is distant from present conditions; therefore, it is not said to be newly acquired.
This intention is easy to understand.

Regarding the "three produced through cultivation": although the roots of goodness such as faith have not previously manifested, they now arise for the first time by relying on conditions such as pure teaching; therefore, they are said to be newly produced.
Therefore, the treatise states: "Because they lack non-conceptual wisdom.

Regarding the fourth [point], the cultivation that gives rise to what is originally present: the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is hidden within the various entanglements; ordinary beings are thus deluded, remaining therein without awakening to it.
If it were non-existent when one is deluded, it could not be called "existent"; thus, the *Nirākāra-śāstra* states: "If it were existent, it should be seen.
Furthermore, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it says: "Because there is attainment and non-attainment, seeing and non-seeing, and so forth."

Now that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) has been attained, the dharmakāya—which was previously obscured by defilements—is for the first time manifested as pure. Previously, it lacked the power to function in the same way as the unconditioned dharmas; now, having attained its functional capacity, it differs from its prior state of non-existence. Therefore, it cannot be said to be "originally existent" (*mūla-sat*), but is rather described as "purified through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-viśuddha*).
Question:
If it is said that what is manifested for the first time as being produced through cultivation is called "cultivation-born," how can it be said to be "manifested"? Answer:

This is solely to clarify that within the gate of cultivation through practice (*pratipatti-mukha*), the meaning of original existence (*prakṛti-siddha*) is established; previously, while the mind was in a state of delusion, the essence and function were not discussed, but now it is finally stated that this Dharmakāya exists. Therefore, one should know that its relationship with the newly arisen [nature] is intimate, whereas its relationship with the previously existing [deluded state] is remote.
As the treatise states: "Whether separated or not separated, it is impermanent.
Since it is called impermanent, it cannot have existed from the beginning.
The four meanings discussed above are all generally applicable here to the reality of the nature of dependent origination.
If one were to categorize the textual divisions of the sutra, these ten cycles of dependent origination consist of only two gates:

first, that which is produced through cultivation; second, that which is produced through cultivation and is inherently existent. The remaining two are found in the "Chapter on the Arising of Nature."
Regarding the second [section], the analysis of the dependent origination of defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), there are two meanings:
first, the gate of dependent origination within the one mind; second, the gate of the supporting basis within the one mind.
As for the gate of dependent origination, it is broadly divided into three parts:

First, the section on the conditional aggregation of the true and the false; second, the section on subsuming the fundamental within the derivative; third, the section on subsuming the derivative within the fundamental.

Regarding "conditional aggregation," this refers generally to the twelve links of dependent origination, wherein the single fundamental consciousness functions such that there is no distinction between the true and the false.
As the treatise states: "Based on the single dharma of mind, there are two gates, for these two gates are not separate from one another.
Furthermore, this sutra says: "Because it is the transformation of mind alone."
Furthermore, as the treatise states: "The union of the real and the delusory is called the *ālaya*.
The real alone does not give rise [to phenomena], nor can the delusory alone be established; it is only through the union of the real and the delusory that there is anything that functions."
Just as with events in a dream, one knows that they arise only when combined with sleep;
this is the gateway to the conditional aggregation of the true and the false.
Second, regarding the subsuming of the fundamental by the derivative: it is because only the deluded mind acts [to produce them].
The treatise states: "It is called the seed-consciousness and the retribution-consciousness.

At the time of the path of counteraction, the fundamental consciousness is entirely exhausted. The dharma-body transmigrating through the five destinies is termed a sentient being; according to the place of its transmigration, it assumes its particular flavor.
The various sufferings within the category of dharmas are not limited to these alone; thus we know that the root is subsumed by its branches.
Question:
When following along with defilement, is it identical to defilement, or does it arise from purity?
Answer: Its essence is pure, and its source is likewise pure; it cannot be termed "following" [defilement]. Therefore, one knows that at the time of defilement, it cannot be called pure.
If this were so, one should not say that the mind of arising and ceasing depends upon the *tathāgatagarbha*; rather, it should be merely a single instance of arising and ceasing.

Now, regarding the statement on mutual dependence: such an explanation is made by one who possesses wisdom and has realized both defilement and purity; therefore, this statement is not restricted solely to the gate of defilement.

Third, as for subsuming the derivative from the fundamental: the twelve links of dependent origination are produced solely by the true mind, just as waves are produced by water, and just as dream-objects are produced solely by the retributive mind, because of the nature of reality.
The Sūtra states: "The five aggregates, the twelve links of dependent origination, ignorance, and all such dharmas are entirely the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, this same Sūtra says: "The three realms are illusory; they are created by the single mind alone."
The commentary on the treatise states: "Because it is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). Question:
Since subsuming the branches under the root should pertain to the category of purity, why is it instead analyzed within the section on defilement?
Answer: This [classification] subsumes the derivative from the fundamental; logically, it belongs to the category of the pure (*śukla-pakṣa*) as dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
However, because it is now intended to contrast with the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) in order to reveal that the defiled is like an illusion, it is placed within the section on the defiled.
Question:

If this is the meaning, then all pure dharmas are equally manifested as false in contrast to the defiled; why then do you specifically distinguish that "gathering the branches back to the root" occurs only within the context of arising from defiled conditions?
Answer: Generally, when discussing the dependent origination of the pure category (*śukla-pakṣa*), there are two aspects.

First, it is to manifest the nature of delusive phenomena in contrast to defilement; thus, a sutra states: "Because one does not know the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the various truths as they truly are."

The second merely reveals the dependent origination of the pure category (*śukla-pakṣa*), which is itself a gateway for revealing the principle (*tattva*); examples include the "Universal Worthy" (*Samantabhadra*) and the "Nature-Arising" (*Tathāgatotpatti-nirdeśa*) chapters.
The remaining meanings may be understood by analogy with this.
This is the subsuming of the derivative from the fundamental, which is precisely the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha.
Within this, there is also the meaning of emptiness, in the sense that its own essence is empty; this shall be analyzed later.

Second, regarding the gate of the single mind as the support: the sixth and seventh consciousnesses and so forth are established based upon the ālaya-vijñāna. Thus, the treatise states: "The twelvefold dependent origination depends upon the ālaya-vijñāna, because the ālaya-vijñāna serves as the universal cause."
Question: How is this distinguished from the "one mind" (ekacitta) of the aforementioned dependent origination? Answer:
Regarding the superior dependent origination within the single mind, defilement and purity are identical in essence and not distinguished as different.
This is the gate of support and maintenance; because the subject and object are distinct, it is divided into two.
Question:
Since the various meanings above are each distinct according to their respective categories, how can they constitute a single realized realm?
Answer:

All that has been explained above is presented according to the distinctions among conditions; that is, the conditions for the path of expedient means (*upāyamārga*) that realizes the object of cognition.
Since these inclinations and desires are distinct, the gates of contemplation (*vipaśyanāmukha*) upon which one now relies are not one.
If one seeks to verify the object of realization, it is as explained above regarding the ten kinds of equality.
The second section, the gate of explaining the meaning, is hereby concluded.
Next, we shall explain the specific characteristics of the gate of contemplation according to the text.

Within the ten contemplations of the original sūtra, the first clarifies the forward contemplation (*anuloma-vipaśyanā*) and the next distinguishes the reverse contemplation (*pratiloma-vipaśyanā*); all others are the same as these.
The characteristics of the reverse contemplation shall be explained later.
Regarding the sequence of the initial section on causes and conditions, there are three types of analysis:
first, clarifying the obstacles to be remedied; second, discerning the essence of contemplation; and third, explaining the scriptural text. All other sections follow this same pattern.

Regarding the statement "remedying the obstacles," this refers to remedying the grasping at a self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), which is the claim that the twelve links [of dependent origination] are created by a self; this is precisely the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) that pervade all [realms].
If the text were divided separately, it would merely remedy the view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*); however, this delusion is common to what is remedied by those three types of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
What are the objects of treatment?
In reality, there is no mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*); yet one perceives a real mark of a person—this is what is treated by the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Dependent origination appears as the arising of a self, yet it does not arise in the manner it is grasped; to reckon this as a semblance-mark (*pratibhāsa-nimitta*) is what is treated by the gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
How is this known?

Because there exists that which resembles the self, the treatise states: "The consciousness that differentiates between self and others arises from the habitual perfuming of the view of self. Thus, it is known.
The manifestation of the characteristics of both apparent and real dharmas is the gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), which universally remedies the two aforementioned attachments.
It can also remedy that [notion of] selflessness and emptiness, as well as the views and characteristics of the eight masteries.
How is this known?
Therefore, the Treatise says: "That which is empty of self-nature exists; thus it establishes the nature of being without intrinsic nature.
This refers to the gateway for treating afflictions.
Regarding the second, the essence of contemplation: this reveals the meaning of the sequential arising of the principle of dependent origination.

Taking the three natures—emptiness, the semblance of reality, and so forth—as the essence of contemplation in the forward order, the reverse order constitutes the contemplation of the single nature of dependent origination as emptiness and lack of intrinsic nature; thus, the principle of the sequential order of dependent origination serves as the essence of this contemplation.
This is explained according to the Sūtra.
If explained according to the Śāstra, it is simply subsumed under "reflection" (cintā).
Third, regarding the analysis of the text: as for that which pertains to the section on causes and conditions (hetu-pratyaya), this refers to the "cause-portion" (hetu-bhāga).
"Successive" (*anupūrva*) means gradual progression.
"Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) means the sense of illuminating and penetrating.
This is how the chapter is titled.
This text consists of four sections, which may be grouped into three according to their characteristics, reduced to two in essence, and subsumed as one in total.
As for the four distinct gates: first, the gate of raising the opponent's misconceptions and clarifying the realization of non-self;
second, the gate of rebuking emotional attachments to reveal the underlying principle, based on the *Śāstra*’s section following "ignorance" and the *Sūtra*’s section following "all ordinary beings."

Third, from "lack of wisdom" (*ajñāna*) in the *Śāstra* down to "constantly following wrong thoughts" (*mithyāmanasikāra*) in the *Sūtra*, is the section on "Discerning Characteristics to Reveal Reality.
Fourth, from "not knowing the various truths and the ultimate truth" (*paramārthasatya*) onwards, is the section on "Discerning Characteristics Based on Reality."
Regarding the three aspects of mutual conformity: among the four gates, the first is termed "establishment";
within the explanation of establishing non-self, the second is termed "response," which is the response that reveals non-self;
and the last is termed "aspect," meaning the aspect of dependent origination established based on the two truths.
Regarding the summary of these two: the first three sections primarily manifest the principle of selflessness, which is the nature of dependent origination;
the final section generally manifests the characteristics of dependent origination.
Taken as a whole, they constitute the sequential order of the first part, the Section on Dependent Origination.

Regarding the third section, "Distinguishing Characteristics to Reveal Reality," it is solely through delusion and craving that the various formations leading up to old age and death arise, and not by means of a self.
Within this, there is first the forward order, followed by the reverse order, and finally the conclusion.

Regarding the initial statement in the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* concerning "ignorance regarding existence and non-existence," the Sūtra says, "constantly following wrong thoughts"; this refers to the link of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Ignorance is delusion (*moha*); "seeking" is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); seeking permanence is called "existence" (*bhava*), while seeking annihilation is called "non-existence" (*vibhava*).

The phrase "in the past, it was merely delusion" means that, in reality, the past is fully endowed with all afflictions; however, because the power of delusion and craving is particularly strong, they are singled out for mention.
The section beginning with "constantly following" refers to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
There are six phrases regarding formations (*saṃskāra*): the first three phrases concern their transgression, while the latter three concern their essence.
According to the Sūtra, the three phrases concerning the transgression of formations are also the member of ignorance (*avidyā*), because they lack the member of ignorance as set forth in the Śāstra.
The phrase "by means of these formations" (*saṃskāra*) refers to the member of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Initially, by means of these formations, the seeds of the mind arise; as the preceding moment gives rise to the succeeding one, the formations permeate the mind, causing the mind to arise subsequently. Therefore, it is called a "seed," and "mind" here refers to the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Second, the section beginning with "with outflows" (sāsrava) clarifies the meaning of the preceding seeds in contrast to subsequent birth and death.
"With outflows" refers to craving (*tṛṣṇā*); "grasping at perceptions" (*saṃjñā-grāha*) refers to views (*dṛṣṭi*).
According to the sūtras, grasping the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) encompasses perception as well.
"Karma as the ground" refers to the subsequent arising of renewed existence (*punarbhava*), which is the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
There are seven phrases regarding the arising of name-and-form and so forth:

first, karma as the ground; second, consciousness as the seed; third, being covered by ignorance (*avidyā*); fourth, being moistened by the water of craving (*tṛṣṇā*); fifth, being irrigated by the mind of self (*ahaṃkāra*); sixth, being bound by the net of various views; and seventh, the sprout of name-and-form arises.
Question:
According to the principle of perfuming (*vāsanā*), karma should be the seed and consciousness the supporting ground; why, then, is consciousness now said to be the seed? Answer:
In general, when discussing the seeds of karma, there are two distinctions:
first, the time when they are formed through perfuming; second, the time when they draw forth and produce the resulting fruit.

If one considers the time when they are formed through perfuming, karma serves as the seed and consciousness serves as the ground; for if consciousness has not yet been perfumed, it cannot be distinguished as having seeds.

Now, regarding perfuming (*vāsanā*), we first speak of seeds giving rise [to effects]. This is closely related to the meaning of the mind as the "perfumer" (*kṣepaka*) mentioned above, whereas its relation to consciousness (*vijñāna*) is remote; therefore, consciousness serves as the ground (*bhūmi*).
The seed is that which depends upon it, and thus belongs to karma.
Regarding the second point, the production that brings about the fruition: consciousness serves as the seed and karma serves as the ground.

What is now referred to as "karma" is the karma-mind of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) seeking birth at the time of impending rebirth; this constitutes the primary karmic seed, which still resides within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) without yet having manifested.

Now, this superior mind seeking birth within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) possesses the characteristic of being a seed; since this characteristic of function is not itself the substance of karma, it can only serve to draw forth the *vijñāna*-link produced by the projecting karma. This is like how the earth draws forth a seed to enable it to produce fruit, yet one speaks of the "earth" as the cause of the karma.

Planted within consciousness, these seeds share the same indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) as that fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). While the preceding mental states of the karma-forming consciousness have already ceased, the present seeds and their manifestations now coexist with the fundamental consciousness. Because they are closely related to consciousness in meaning, whereas they are distantly related to the perfuming agents (*vāsana*), they are determined to be seeds by being integrated with consciousness itself.
This has two meanings:
